title: Classroom Management Is Easy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Marking the site's 80th article, this piece argues that effective classroom management should feel easy rather than exhausting, and that difficulty is a sign of using the wrong approach rather than insufficient effort. Linsin frames classroom management as fundamentally knowledge-based - rewarding teachers who know the right predictable levers rather than those who simply work hardest - and describes rules and consequences as only a small piece of the larger picture, which also includes building rapport, creating leverage, and being an effective storyteller. He lists a series of "old methods" teachers should be able to abandon entirely: persuading, bribing, yelling, arguing, debating, negotiating, lecturing, scolding, glaring, and threatening. The article closes by reiterating that stress and hard work are themselves diagnostic signs that something in a teacher's approach needs to change.
points: Effective classroom management is framed as knowledge-based, rewarding teachers who know the right techniques rather than those who simply work hardest.
Rules and consequences are described as only a small part of overall classroom management, alongside rapport, leverage, and storytelling.
A list of "old methods" - persuading, bribing, yelling, arguing, negotiating, lecturing, scolding, glaring, threatening - should be entirely unnecessary with the right approach.
Feeling stressed or like classroom management is hard work is presented as a diagnostic sign that something needs to change.
quotes: Classroom management should feel easy. If it feels difficult to you, if it feels like you’re straining and working to get students to behave and pay attention, then you’re doing something wrong.
Effective classroom management is knowledge based. Unlike most successes in life, it doesn’t reward those who work the hardest. It rewards those who work the smartest.
Students react predictably-both good and bad-to certain teacher behaviors, techniques, and strategies. Knowing which is which is like having a key that unlocks the secrets to happy teaching.

Rules and consequences are an important part of classroom management. There is no getting around it. You can’t be an effective teacher without an unwavering commitment to following them. But they’re only a small part of classroom management—just a sliver.
You have to know how to create leverage, how to build rapport, how to get students excited about coming to school, how to be an effective storyteller, and how to get students to want to behave.
You shouldn’t have to persuade, bribe, yell, argue, debate, negotiate, lecture, scold, glare, or threaten students to behave.
But most important, classroom management shouldn’t be stressful. If it is, or if it feels like hard work, or if you find yourself using any of these old methods, then you’re doing something wrong.
